fatal_errors: The proposed Ni addition does not reconstruct the liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h.
It incorrectly treats the starting material as an already formed W–Cu composite with voids rather than a single-BCC WTaVTi dendrite–interdendrite precursor.
It omits the central selective Ti extraction/Cu replacement mechanism, retained RHEA ligaments, and spontaneously formed W-rich passivating interlayer.
Claims of performance under fusion neutron/gamma irradiation are unsupported; the target evidence was limited to 25 keV He+ irradiation of precursor dendrites as a proxy, not the finished composite.
No prior evidence is cited for Ni suppressing phase separation or improving net thermal conductivity in this system, and Ni could itself introduce alloying and electron-scattering penalties.
The intervention is not uniquely specified because Ni coating and bulk powder blending can produce materially different structures and mechanisms.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad engineering themes of W/Cu interfacial integrity and thermal transport, and its controlled comparison with microscopy and laser-flash measurements would be reasonably falsifiable. However, it misses essentially every defining feature of the target: the WTaVTi precursor, molten-Cu liquid-metal dealloying, directional selective replacement of Ti/V-rich channels, bicontinuous RHEA–Cu architecture, W-rich interlayer, measured temperature-dependent conductivity, and restricted He-irradiation evidence. Its predicted conductivity improvement is only a generic directional match. The stated 300–1000 °C neutron/gamma service boundary extrapolates far beyond any supplied evidence, while the absence of supporting citations prevents treating Ni modification as a well-supported alternative.
